title: Store stove heat for the night: water, brick and masonry
summary: Mass warmed by the stove gives heat back after the fire dies down. Water holds about four and a half times as much per kilogram as brick, but masonry runs hotter and real storage weighs hundreds of kilograms to tonnes. Keep mass outside the stove's clearances, put heavy mass where the floor can carry it, and never sleep over a smoke flue without a CO alarm.

materials.item: Plastic jugs, pails or a steel drum that held only water, caps left loose
materials.qty: as many as the floor allows

materials.item: Firebrick for anything the fire touches
Non-combustible base: sheet steel, tile or a slab
CO alarm for each sleeping area

steps.text: Work out what you are asking for: every 1 kWh is about 43 L of water cooling 20 °C, or about 200 kg of brick cooling 20 °C (USGS water, ETB specific heat). Water and loose brick kept outside the clearances may only swing about that much (our estimate); only masonry built round the fire runs far hotter.
steps.warn: A few jugs only take the edge off. Real overnight storage is hundreds of kilograms.

steps.text: Place water containers or stacked brick outside the stove's clearance zone: the label distance, or 1,200 mm (48 in) for an unlabelled stove (NRCan wood heating). Those distances are to things that burn, so they don't say how close plain brick may go; this card keeps it outside them too as the cautious default.

Use plastic jugs, pails or drums of water with the caps loose. A drum should be one that held only water, as for the [barrel stove](#guides/build_barrel_stove); anything else goes through the [hot-work card](#guides/safety_hot_work_containers) first.
steps.warn: Never a sealed container or glass jar near heat: heated closed containers burst.

steps.text: Stack brick or stone dry on a non-combustible base, not touching the stove and not blocking its air or any shield's air gap.

Check the floor before anything heavy goes on it: Canada's joist span tables assume a live load of up to 1.9 kPa, about 194 kg per square metre (our arithmetic), of people and furniture spread over the floor (NRC 9.23.4.1). It is a design figure, not a measured limit, and not meant for a standing mass. A full 208 L drum puts about four and a half times that on its footprint (Repackify drums), and a masonry heater weighs at least 800 kg (MHA definition).
steps.warn: Put heavy mass on a concrete slab or ground, or over a wall or beam below. Stop if the floor sags or cracks.

steps.text: Run the stove as usual, never smouldering, and let the mass carry the heat after it dies down. A masonry heater wants one or two short, hot fires a day (NRCan wood heating, MHA definition).

For a masonry heater, build on a concrete or solid-masonry footing at least 305 mm (12 in) thick, below frost depth, with 914 mm (36 in) to anything that burns and 1,220 mm (48 in) in front of the door (MHA builders, quoting the US International Residential Code). In Canada NRCan says a masonry heater's clearances must meet the building code's standards for conventional fireplaces, so check those too (NRCan wood heating).
steps.warn: NRCan says a well-working masonry heater is hard to build without specialised training (NRCan wood heating).

steps.text: For a rocket mass heater or a heated bench, follow Evans and Jackson's book and treat it as an uncertified, experimental stove: uncertified clearances, a proper chimney and a CO alarm (Oasis woodheat, NRCan wood heating).
Never sleep over a smoke flue without a working CO alarm in the room, close enough to wake you (China CDC CO).
steps.warn: In Korea, coal-briquette CO poisoned an estimated 26 million people from 1951 to 2018 and killed about 65,000; in one survey most cases came from ondol floor heating (Kim 2020).

steps.text: Fire a heated bed hot in the evening and let it burn down well before sleep. Don't add fuel or turn the air down for the night: in Korea briquettes were changed just before sleep and air holes closed to stretch the burn, which made more CO while people slept (Kim 2020).
steps.warn: A coal briquette's CO peaked 2 to 3 hours after it was lit, so one changed just before bed peaked in deep sleep (Kim 2020). Kim studied briquettes, not wood.

steps.text: Close a damper only when the fire is completely out and the ashes are cold (Calgary fireplaces).
Every week, look over masonry, cob and flues for cracks, soot stains and smoke smell, and seal them before the next fire.
Keep babies, the frail, people with numb feet and anyone drunk or sedated off heated beds and away from hot masonry.

notes:
## How much heat mass holds
Heat stored = mass × specific heat × the drop in temperature. 1 kWh is 3,600 kJ.

| Material | Specific heat, kJ per kg per °C | Density, kg/m³ | Roughly kJ per litre of bulk per °C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Water | 4.18 (USGS water) | 1,000 | 4.2 |
| Common brick | 0.9 | 1,400 to 2,400 | 1.7 at 1,900 kg/m³ |
| Firebrick | 1.05 | 1,800 to 2,200 | 2.1 at 2,000 kg/m³ |
| Stone | 0.84 | 2,300 to 2,800 | 2.1 at 2,500 kg/m³ |
| Dense concrete | 0.92 (UCCS appendix 5) | 2,000 to 2,400 | 2.0 at 2,200 kg/m³ |
| Dry sand | 0.80 | 1,400 to 1,600 | 1.2 at 1,500 kg/m³ |

Specific heats and densities from the sources named (ETB specific heat, ETB density, USGS water, UCCS appendix 5); the last column is our arithmetic. Engineering ToolBox lists 0.75 for 'Concrete, stone' but a university table gives 0.92 for concrete (UCCS appendix 5), so concrete is taken from that. Treat all the masonry figures as approximate.

What that means:
- Per kilogram, water holds about four and a half times what brick does; per litre of space, about two and a half times.
- Water can't pass 100 °C without boiling, and jugs kept a safe distance from the stove probably only get warm (our guess: it depends on the stove and the distance). Masonry built round a fire runs far hotter: MHA's definition of a masonry heater has the outside surface at or below 110 °C (230 °F), except right round the fuel loading door, while the firebox runs above 815 °C (1,500 °F) (MHA definition). That is a design rule, not a promise for a home-built one. Brick makes up for its lower specific heat by swinging through more degrees.
- Worked example: giving the room 1 kW for a 10-hour night is 10 kWh. That is about 430 L of water or 2,000 kg of brick if each cools 20 °C (say 40 to 20 °C). Only if the mass gets much hotter does it drop to about 215 L of water (60 to 20 °C) or 500 kg of brick (100 to 20 °C), and loose mass outside the clearances is unlikely to get that hot (our estimate). A real night may need more or less: your room's loss is the unknown.
- That is why real masonry heaters weigh at least 800 kg (MHA definition), and NRCan describes them as tonnes of brick or stone (NRCan wood heating). A few jugs of water take the edge off; they don't carry a house through a Canadian night.

## Water and brick near the stove
- **Place mass outside the stove's clearance zone**: the label distance, or 1,200 mm (48 in) for an unlabelled stove, the same as furniture and firewood ([Install a salvaged wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install)). It still soaks up radiant heat there and gives it back after the fire dies.
- **Water:** plastic jugs, pails or drums with the caps loose. Never seal a container you heat, and never glass jars: closed containers burst when heated ([heating sealed containers](#browse/hazards/sealed_heating)). Water stored for drinking is a separate supply: don't count on it as mass if you'll need it.
- **Brick and stone:** stacked dry on a non-combustible base, not touching the stove and not blocking its air or any shield's air gap. Brick fixed flat to a wooden wall is not a heat shield and gives no reduction in clearance ([Install a salvaged wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install)).
- **Warm bricks for beds** have their own rules: [Staying warm, warmed bricks](#guides/skill_staying_warm).

## The weight on the floor
Canada's house floor-joist span tables are for floors in residential areas, or where the live load is no more than 1.9 kPa (NRC 9.23.4.1). That is a live load, meaning people and furniture, spread over the whole floor: about 194 kg per square metre (our arithmetic). It is a design figure, not the load a floor fails at, and a standing mass of brick, cob or water is permanent weight on a few joists, not a spread-out live load. A full 208 L (55 US gal) steel drum of water weighs about 225 kg on a footprint 572 mm (22.5 in) across (Repackify drums), about 870 kg per square metre: four and a half times that figure. Nobody can say from here what your floor will carry. A masonry heater is at least 800 kg by MHA's definition: even spread over 1.5 m² of floor that is about 530 kg per square metre, nearly three times the 1.9 kPa figure, and real ones weigh more (MHA definition, our arithmetic). Put heavy mass on a concrete slab or ground, or over a bearing wall or beam below, and watch for a floor that sags, cracks or bounces. In the US code a masonry heater sits on a non-combustible footing of concrete or solid masonry at least 305 mm (12 in) thick, below frost depth; MHA says unlisted heaters must be built on a non-combustible foundation (MHA builders).

## Masonry heaters
A masonry heater is a site-built heater of mainly masonry that stores the heat of short, hot fires (about 2 hours with the firebox above 815 °C) and gives it out for 12 to 24 hours or more (MHA definition). In MHA's definition the smoke turns through at least one 180° bend inside, and the shortest path from firebox to chimney is at least twice the firebox's largest dimension; the doors are tight and stay shut while it burns (MHA definition). MHA says burning fast and hot leaves minimal opportunity for creosote or incomplete combustion in a heater built to its definition (MHA definition); a salvage-built one hasn't been tested. They still need a chimney (MHA builders).

Building one is a mason's job. NRCan says someone without specialised training and plenty of experience would find it difficult to build one that works well and lasts (NRCan wood heating). The rules a salvager must keep if they try anyway (MHA builders, quoting the US International Residential Code; NRCan says Canadian clearances follow the building code's fireplace standards, so check the local code too):
- A concrete or solid-masonry footing below frost depth, as above.
- 914 mm (36 in) to anything that burns, with the space open so air flows round it; 1,220 mm (48 in) in front of the loading door. Thick solid walls earn smaller side clearances under the code exceptions.
- Firebrick wherever fire touches.
- Cutting brick, block and stone makes silica dust: cut wet and outdoors ([silica dust](#browse/hazards/silica)).
- The chimney pulls weakest on cold start-ups and mild days, when smoke can roll back into the room (MHA builders).

## Rocket mass heaters
Ianto Evans and Leslie Jackson's book *Rocket Mass Heaters* (Cob Cottage Company, 3rd edition 2014) is the usual guide to these: a rocket-style fire whose heat is stored in a cob bench, bed or floor, which its publisher says gives gentle heat for up to two days without an all-night smouldering fire. The same review called them experimental, with probably fewer than a hundred in regular use by early 2004, and gives no test data (Oasis woodheat). A home-built one carries no listing, and no code or lab test is cited here for rocket mass heaters, so treat the uncertified-stove clearances as a cautious rule of thumb, not a tested figure. NRCan warns that an uncertified stove may be a serious fire hazard and that you may not be able to get insurance (NRCan wood heating). Treat it like any uncertified stove: the uncertified clearances, a proper chimney, a CO alarm and a floor that can take the weight. If its exhaust runs through a bench or bed people sleep on, the kang and ondol rules below apply to it as well. Rocket fire basics: [Rocket stove](#guides/build_rocket_stove). Drum rules for any steel part: [Barrel stove](#guides/build_barrel_stove).

## Beds over a smoke flue: kang and ondol
A Chinese kang and a Korean ondol run the fire's smoke through channels under a brick or clay bed or floor. The danger is CO leaking up through cracks into the room where people sleep:
- **Korea:** an estimated 26 million people were poisoned by CO from coal briquettes between 1951 and 2018, and about 65,000 died. Ondol rooms inevitably have small leaks; a survey of 1965 to 1976 blamed gas leaking from ondol structures for 54% of poisonings, and about 80% of cases came from ondol heating. Floors heated by flue gas had about 11% of households poisoned a year, against about 7% where hot water in pipes heated the floor instead. Closing the air holes overnight to stretch a briquette made more CO, and a briquette changed just before bed peaked in CO 2 to 3 hours later, in deep sleep (Kim 2020).
- **China:** the national CDC lists heating with a kang (a stove-heated bed) or a fire-heated wall in a poorly ventilated room as a CO risk. It says coal stoves and charcoal fires should not be in the bedroom, and that a CO detector is worth fitting where they are used (China CDC CO).

Most of this was coal briquettes, each burning for hours (Kim 2020), but glowing wood coals make CO too ([Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide)). If you build or use one:
- A working CO alarm in the room, placed where its maker says and close enough to wake the sleepers, and a smoke alarm. An alarm is the last line of defence, not a fix for a leaky bed: see [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide) for what an alarm can't tell you.
- Fire it hot in the evening and let it burn down well before sleep; don't load fresh fuel or turn the air down for the night (Kim 2020, MHA definition).
- Close a damper only when the fire is completely out and the ashes are cold (Calgary fireplaces).
- Inspect the bed's surface and the flue every week for cracks, soot stains and smoke smell, and seal them.
- Hot-water pipes under a bed avoid the smoke flue, and Korea's pipe-heated floors poisoned fewer households than smoke-heated ones, though both burned briquettes (Kim 2020). Don't plumb a stove coil to a floor or bed loop on the strength of this card: a loop lying lower than the stove can't circulate by itself, so it needs a pump, which stops with the power (our reasoning), and the [water coil card](#guides/build_stove_water_coil) covers only a gravity loop to a tank above the coil.

## Who shouldn't sleep on heat
A warm bed is contact heat. Babies, people who can't feel or move away (numb feet, diabetes, the very old), and anyone drunk or sedated can be burned: see [Contact heat](#guides/skill_staying_warm).
